Reference: Grossman and Helpman (1991)

Model Setting

The paper builds a general-equilibrium model of endogenous growth in which the engine of growth is the repeated improvement of a fixed set of products. Earlier one-shot patent-race models (Loury 1979; Lee and Wilde 1980) miss the cyclical nature of quality competition: each product enjoys a limited run at the technological frontier and is then displaced. Segerstrom, Anant and Dinopoulos (1990) and Aghion and Howitt (1990) embed patent races in dynamic general equilibrium, but in the former all research is devoted to one industry at a time in sequence, and in the latter one economy-wide innovation improves all products at once. Here there is a continuum of products, each with its own quality ladder, and entrepreneurs race simultaneously in all industries to bring out the next generation of each product. Individual products climb their ladders stochastically and at different speeds, so a distribution of qualities evolves over time, but by the law of large numbers the aggregate is smooth: an index of consumption grows at a constant rate that can be computed in closed form.

The main findings are four. First, the economy jumps immediately to a steady state in which the intensity of innovation rises with the size of the labour force, with the productivity of research labour and with the size of the quality step, so that R&D responds to profit incentives and the economy exhibits dynamic increasing returns to scale. Second, the market rate of innovation can be either too fast or too slow: a successful innovator creates a positive consumer-surplus and intertemporal-spillover externality and a negative business-stealing externality, and the latter dominates when the steps of the ladder are small or very large. A tax or subsidy on R&D decentralizes the optimum. Third, a model of growth through expanding product variety has exactly the same reduced form as the quality-ladder model, yet its welfare properties differ, because there equilibrium growth is always too slow. Fourth, in a two-factor, two-sector extension only a larger endowment of the factor used intensively in R&D guarantees faster growth, and in a two-country version the long-run pattern of intersectoral trade follows the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem.

Producers

Labour is the only primary input, and one unit of labour produces one unit of any product regardless of quality, so marginal cost equals the wage w(t)w(t)w(t). Firms in an industry compete in prices. If several firms can make the same quality, Bertrand competition drives price to unit cost and profits to zero. If one firm has a quality lead, it charges a price that, adjusted for quality, just undercuts the unit cost of its nearest rival, and it captures the whole market. It does not charge more because it would lose all customers, and it does not charge less because industry demand is unit elastic, so revenue is independent of price while output and cost rise as price falls. In equilibrium every industry has a unique leader exactly one step ahead of its nearest rival, so all state-of-the-art products carry the same limit price and every leader earns the same profit flow:

p=λw,π=(λw−w)Eλw=(1−1λ)E(7)p=\lambda w,\qquad\pi=\left(\lambda w-w\right)\frac{E}{\lambda w}=\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)E \tag{7}p=λw,π=(λw−w)λwE​=(1−λ1​)E(7)

since demand per product is E/λwE/\lambda wE/λw. A blueprint is needed to produce any quality. Patents are infinitely lived and licensing is not feasible, so only the firm that developed the state-of-the-art product manufactures it. The same outcome arises without patents if imitation is costly, since an imitator would earn zero profit in the ensuing Bertrand equilibrium.

R&D Races

An entrepreneur may target any product. Research at intensity ι~\tilde{\iota}ι~ for an interval of length dtdtdt succeeds in taking the next step up the ladder with probability ι~dt\tilde{\iota}dtι~dt and requires aIι~a_I\tilde{\iota}aI​ι~ units of labour per unit of time. Success is therefore a Poisson process whose arrival rate depends only on current R&D activity, not on past effort. Entry into every race is free, and the input requirement aIa_IaI​ is the same for incumbents and newcomers: by inspecting the goods on the market, outsiders learn enough to work on the next generation even though they cannot produce the current one. This is the public-good aspect of technology in the model.

Leaders do not try to improve their own products. A leader that succeeded would be two steps ahead and could charge λ2w\lambda^2wλ2w, so its incremental profit would be:

Δπ=(1−1λ2)E−(1−1λ)E=(1−1λ)Eλ(8)\Delta\pi=\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\right)E-\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)E=\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)\frac{E}{\lambda} \tag{8}Δπ=(1−λ21​)E−(1−λ1​)E=(1−λ1​)λE​(8)

which is strictly less than the gain (1−1/λ)E(1-1/\lambda)E(1−1/λ)E of a non-leader who succeeds. With a perfectly elastic supply of challengers, leaders cannot compete for financing; a leader would rather use research funds to gain leadership in another industry. This also confirms that every lead is exactly one step. Since π\piπ is the same in all industries, entrepreneurs are indifferent among targets when leadership is expected to last equally long everywhere, and the paper studies the symmetric equilibrium in which every product is targeted with the same aggregate intensity ι\iotaι.

Let vvv be the stock-market value of a leader, the present value of its uncertain profit stream. An entrepreneur obtains vvv with probability ι~dt\tilde{\iota}dtι~dt at cost waIι~dtwa_I\tilde{\iota}dtwaI​ι~dt. The risk is idiosyncratic, so she maximizes the expected net benefit vι~dt−waIι~dtv\tilde{\iota}dt-wa_I\tilde{\iota}dtvι~dt−waI​ι~dt, which is linear in ι~\tilde{\iota}ι~. v=waI(9)v=wa_I \tag{9}v=waI​(9)

This risk is also idiosyncratic, so the expected return must equal the safe interest rate. The no-arbitrage condition and its form after substituting free entry are:

A larger LLL shifts LLLLLL out, which is a pure resource effect. A lower aIa_IaI​ shifts LLLLLL out and ΠΠ\Pi\PiΠΠ down, so that a resource effect and an incentive effect work in the same direction. A larger economy grows faster, as in Romer (1990) and Aghion and Howitt (1990): the cost of a blueprint is fixed while the profit flow it earns scales with the size of the market.

Market incentives for R&D are excessive when the steps of the quality ladder are quite small or quite large, and insufficient for steps of intermediate size. Under-investment is more likely when L/aIL/a_IL/aI​ is large, that is, in economies that are large in units of research-efficiency labour.

The intuition compares the externalities of a marginal innovation, in the utility metric. On the positive side, consumers pay the same price as before and receive a product of higher quality. This gain lasts while the innovator keeps her lead (the consumer-surplus effect) and also indefinitely afterwards, because every later innovation builds on a product one step higher than otherwise (the intertemporal-spillover effect). On the negative side, the innovator destroys the producer surplus of the leader she displaces (the business-stealing effect), and the loss is multiplied because the owners' lower income reduces demand and profits for all other leaders: the displaced flow is the profit share 1−1/λ1-1/\lambda1−1/λ of spending, and the multiplier is λ\lambdaλ, so instantaneous profits of others fall by λ−1\lambda-1λ−1 per unit of spending. This flow is discounted at ι+ρ\iota+\rhoι+ρ, the effective discount rate for profits. The two totals are:

log⁡λρandλ−1ι+ρ(20)\frac{\log\lambda}{\rho}\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\lambda-1}{\iota+\rho} \tag{20}ρlogλ​andι+ρλ−1​(20)

Evaluated at the market value of ι\iotaι, their difference has the same sign as ι∗−ι\iota^*-\iotaι∗−ι. For λ\lambdaλ just above λ0\lambda_0λ0​ innovation is close to zero, so both flows are discounted at nearly the same rate and λ−1>log⁡λ\lambda-1>\log\lambdaλ−1>logλ makes business stealing dominate; for very large λ\lambdaλ the displaced profits grow linearly in λ\lambdaλ while the utility gain grows only logarithmically. A larger ι\iotaι shortens the period over which the displaced profits would have been earned and so reduces the business-stealing effect without changing the consumer-surplus effect.

The optimum can be decentralized by a tax or subsidy on R&D outlays. Let TTT be the multiple of R&D costs borne by the firm, with T>1T>1T>1 a tax and T<1T<1T<1 a subsidy. Free entry becomes v=TaIv=Ta_Iv=TaI​, and the steady-state no-arbitrage condition is replaced by:

Quality versus Variety

The paper compares the quality ladder with growth through an expanding range of horizontally differentiated products (Romer 1990; Grossman and Helpman 1989, 1990). Lifetime utility is unchanged, but the consumption index exhibits love of variety as in Dixit and Stiglitz (1977):

The second equation is labour-market clearing, with (aD/n)n˙(a_D/n)\dot{n}(aD​/n)n˙ workers in R&D and n(E/np)=αEn(E/np)=\alpha En(E/np)=αE in manufacturing. The economy again jumps to the steady state where (1−α)E/aD=ρ+γ(1-\alpha)E/a_D=\rho+\gamma(1−α)E/aD​=ρ+γ.

The variety model is the quality model with γ\gammaγ in place of ι\iotaι, aDa_DaD​ in place of aIa_IaI​ and α\alphaα in place of 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ, so every positive comparative static carries over. In both models agents invest to acquire the exclusive ability to make a new product, and in both R&D generates a spillover that is not appropriated. In the variety model the spillover is explicit, since each new product lowers the cost of later R&D; in the quality model it is implicit, since once one improvement succeeds other researchers can drop that project and start on the next step.

Result (variety growth is too slow). Whenever the optimal rate of innovation is positive, it exceeds the market rate. A new product initially adds (1−α)En1/α−2(1-\alpha)En^{1/\alpha-2}(1−α)En1/α−2 to consumer surplus. The marginal entrant inflicts an aggregate loss of profits of (1−α)E/αn(1-\alpha)E/\alpha n(1−α)E/αn on the nnn existing firms, and the marginal utility of income is αn1/α−1\alpha n^{1/\alpha-1}αn1/α−1. The static consumer-surplus and business-stealing effects therefore cancel exactly, a property of constant-elasticity preferences first noted by Dixit and Stiglitz (1977), and both compound in the same way over time. What remains is the intertemporal spillover through which current innovation lowers the cost of later R&D, so the marginal innovation conveys a net positive externality. In the quality model, by contrast, the two static effects do not cancel and the sign of the net externality depends on λ\lambdaλ.

In the plane with wHw_HwH​ on the horizontal axis and ι\iotaι on the vertical axis, the first equation is an upward-sloping curve HHHHHH (a higher skilled wage releases skilled labour from the other two activities) and the second is a downward-sloping curve ΠΠ\Pi\PiΠΠ (a higher skilled wage raises the cost of R&D relative to sales).

Result (factor composition and growth). An increase in HHH shifts HHHHHH up and leaves ΠΠ\Pi\PiΠΠ unchanged, so innovation and growth rise: accumulating the factor used intensively in R&D is conducive to growth. An increase in LLL shifts both curves to the right, and ι\iotaι rises if and only if ΠΠ\Pi\PiΠΠ shifts by more, which happens if and only if the elasticity of substitution σ\sigmaσ between skilled and unskilled labour in the outside good exceeds one. The shift of ΠΠ\Pi\PiΠΠ is the change in wHw_HwH​ that keeps Y(wH,L)/wHY(w_H,L)/w_HY(wH​,L)/wH​ constant; the shift of HHHHHH is larger than this exactly when HYH_YHY​ rises with LLL at constant Y/wHY/w_HY/wH​, which holds if and only if θH+ϵH>1\theta_H+\epsilon_H>1θH​+ϵH​>1, where θH\theta_HθH​ is the cost share of skilled labour in YYY and ϵH\epsilon_HϵH​ is the absolute elasticity of its marginal product; and θH+ϵH=1+ϵH(1−σ)\theta_H+\epsilon_H=1+\epsilon_H(1-\sigma)θH​+ϵH​=1+ϵH​(1−σ). Intuitively, a larger outside sector draws skilled labour away from R&D through an output effect, but the rise in wHw_HwH​ releases skilled labour through a substitution effect, which dominates when σ>1\sigma>1σ>1. In a second special case all three activities use the factors in fixed proportions, with R&D the most and the outside good the least skill intensive; then an increase in unskilled labour must slow growth. A positive link between resources and growth therefore holds only for particular general-equilibrium structures.

International Trade

Two countries, home and foreign (foreign variables carry an asterisk), share the two-factor, two-sector structure. First suppose a differentiated product must be manufactured where its latest improvement was made, which rules out licensing and multinationals. The benchmark is the integrated equilibrium, the equilibrium of the previous block for a world without borders. In a box whose sides are the world endowments of HHH and LLL, one vector gives integrated-equilibrium employment in the combined activity of R&D and manufacturing of XXX, namely aIι+aXXa_I\iota+a_XXaI​ι+aX​X, and the other gives employment in the outside good; together with their mirror images they form a parallelogram.

Result (replication of the integrated equilibrium). If the endowment point lies inside this parallelogram, there is a free-trade equilibrium with factor prices, interest rates, commodity prices and all aggregate quantities equal to those of the integrated equilibrium. The proof is by construction. At integrated-equilibrium factor prices techniques are the same in both countries, and each country's endowment can be fully employed by a unique non-negative split between the combined activity and the outside good. The home country manufactures a measure nnn of the differentiated products, performs the fraction nnn of world R&D and so keeps leadership in a measure nnn of products in every period; the foreign country accounts for n∗=1−nn^*=1-nn∗=1−n. All activities break even and the no-arbitrage condition holds in each country, world income is unchanged, and homothetic preferences make the distribution of income irrelevant for demand, so product markets clear. Trade in goods alone, with or without trade in financial assets, suffices.

Result (pattern of trade). Without trade in financial assets, trade is balanced. Demand has the same composition in both countries, and the country abundant in unskilled labour specializes relatively in the outside good, so the skill-abundant country imports the outside good and is a net exporter of differentiated products, with intra-industry trade within that sector. This is the Heckscher-Ohlin prediction, now for the steady state of an economy with continual quality upgrading. Unlike the closed economy, the world economy does not jump to the steady state unless initial ownership of frontier blueprints happens to equal nnn and n∗n^*n∗. If financial assets are traded during the adjustment, steady-state trade is generally not balanced, and a country with a large enough surplus on the service account may import the outside good and, on net, differentiated products; an imbalance cannot, however, reverse the Heckscher-Ohlin pattern. Finally, if R&D and manufacturing may be located in different countries, firms have no reason to separate them inside the parallelogram. Outside it, when R&D is more skill intensive than manufacturing, multinational corporations that do research at home and manufacture abroad can restore the integrated equilibrium for a further set of endowments, and for some endowments beyond that set multinationals still emerge but the equilibrium differs from the integrated one.

Two consequences are used throughout. Perfect substitution within a product means that only the quality with the lowest quality-adjusted price is bought, and that a leader can drive out a rival by limit pricing (equations (4) and (7)).
